comparison: Both address behavioral evidence for sequence structure differences (C3, C4, C26, C28-C31, C35-C36, C41). OpenEval finds the evidence SUPPORTED with converging measures and appropriate statistics. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising critical concerns about whether behavior represents true chunking versus increased checking behavior, requesting analysis of sequence variability and stereotypy.

Both evaluate lever hold experiment data (C42-C51). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with consistent behavioral data and appropriate statistical analyses demonstrating temporal constraints. Peer reviewers also find SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 1 describing the study as 'excellent' and Reviewer 3 noting 'behavioral analysis is novel and strong.' No specific challenges to these claims.

Both address speed and inter-press-interval findings (C52-C58, C74). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by timestamp and acoustic data with statistical confirmation. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting chunking analyses 'rely on visual interpretation' and requesting 'quantitative methods to assess group differences' and proportional analyses, concluding data may not provide evidence of different chunking.

Both evaluate detailed temporal analysis of inter-press-intervals and chunking patterns (C59-C77). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with strong converging evidence from visual and quantitative analyses. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, stating analyses 'rely on visual interpretation' and that 'aged mice simply perform many more sequences,' suggesting proportional analyses may be needed and questioning whether groups differ in chunking versus overall lever pressing.

Both address neuronal mapping and p-MAPK data (C80-C94). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with extensive data and appropriate statistical analyses showing age-related corticostriatal deficits. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising major concerns that circuit activity 'may be inherently confounded by general differences in lever pressing' and questioning whether groups are matched for total lever presses, undermining confidence in neural circuit conclusions.

Both evaluate chemogenetic experiments (C101-C121). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, noting well-controlled experiments with appropriate validation and interpretation of partial recapitulation. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, with all three reviewers expressing concerns that manipulation 'reproduced some features' but 'did not recapitulate the full or even most of the phenotype,' questioning high CNO dose, noting inconsistencies in data presentation, and stating 'There are no data to support' that disrupted dSPN activity underlies aged deficits.

Both address feedback cue intervention experiment (C124-C139). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with well-designed experiment and appropriate controls demonstrating cognitive-motor nature of deficit. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising concerns that auditory cue 'may also act as a conditioned reinforcer' (different hypothesis), and critically questioning whether aged C57 mice have hearing impairment that could explain all differences in sequence performance.

Both evaluate control experiments on sensory detection (C37-C40) and sequence trigger learning (C32-C33). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, confirming sensory detection intact and that aged mice learned contingencies. Peer reviewers also find SUPPORTED, though Reviewer 2 requests additional data on how well mice met sequence trigger. The magazine training data showing equivalent learning is not directly challenged.

Both address general learning capacity and motivation (C24-C25). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with appropriate mixed ANOVA showing intact general learning. Peer reviewers also find SUPPORTED, with no specific challenges to this basic behavioral finding. Reviewers note the task is 'elegant and carefully designed' and 'behavioral analysis is novel and strong.'

Both address sequence trigger learning (C32-C33). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED showing aged mice learned contingencies but implemented differently. Peer reviewers find SUPPORTED, though Reviewer 2 requests additional data on how well mice met the sequence trigger, noting 'It is possible that the aged mice never learned the contingency.'

Both address correlation analyses linking behavioral and neuronal measures (C5, C87, C157). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with appropriate acknowledgment that correlation cannot establish causation. Peer reviewers rate the broader neural circuit analysis UNCERTAIN due to methodological concerns about confounding by general lever pressing differences.

Both address integration of chemogenetic findings with literature (C6, C158, C178-C179). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, noting consistency with cited work while extending to aging. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, with concerns that the manuscript 'implies that disrupted DLS D1 MSN activity underlies the deficits in aged mice. There are no data to support this.'

Both address feedback cue experiment and clinical implications (C7, C189). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with clear demonstration of temporary restoration. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising concerns about hearing impairment in aged C57 mice potentially explaining results and questioning whether auditory cue acts as conditioned reinforcer rather than action feedback.

Both evaluate main conclusions integrating behavioral and neuronal findings (C8-C9, C185-C186, C188). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by convergence of evidence from multiple experiments. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, requesting clarification on 'why one would think the microchunking in the aged mice is a form of habit,' questioning whether behavior represents true automaticity, and noting hearing impairment concerns challenge interpretations.

OpenEval evaluates hypothesis about dSPN involvement (C100) as SUPPORTED, noting it was reasonable and subsequently tested with partial support from chemogenetic experiments. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this hypothesis claim.

Both address integration with human literature (C143-C145). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with appropriate comparison across species. Peer reviewers rate the broader conclusions UNCERTAIN, questioning the interpretation framework and requesting clarification on why microchunking would be considered habit or model-free learning.

Both address p-MAPK mapping showing widespread correlations and reduced activation patterns (C156, C165-C166). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, noting novel insight into aging effects. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN due to methodological concerns about potential confounding by general lever pressing differences.

Both evaluate interpretive conclusions about intact learning capacity with different automaticity implementation (C162-C164). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by feedback cue experiment showing aged mice can execute long sequences with cues. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, questioning the interpretation framework and raising hearing impairment concerns that could provide alternative explanation.

OpenEval evaluates speculative interpretations (C89, C122, C150, C155, C166, C169-C170, C173, C175-C176, C183) as UNCERTAIN, appropriately noting these are hypotheses not directly tested. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these speculative claims as a group.

OpenEval evaluates established knowledge from literature (C1-C2, C10-C21, C78-C79, C81, C95-C99, C140-C142, C146-C149, C151-C154, C167-C168, C172, C174, C177, C180-C181) as SUPPORTED by appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these background/context claims.
OpenEval evaluates methodological details about age selection (C22-C23) as SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these basic methodological claims.

OpenEval evaluates acknowledgment of chemogenetic limitation (C182) as SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers raise related concerns about CNO dose and effects, but no specific evaluation addresses this limitation claim directly.
OpenEval evaluates statements about broader significance and clinical applications (C187, C190) as SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers do not specifically evaluate these forward-looking claims.

Both address visual analysis showing both groups learned to form sequences (C34-C35). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as important baseline. Peer reviewers raise concerns about the broader interpretation of what these sequences represent (chunking vs. checking), but do not directly challenge that sequences were formed.

Both note differences between chemogenetic model and natural aging (C115). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, viewing this as consistent with partial recapitulation. Peer reviewers raise this as a concern, noting the manipulation 'did not recapitulate the full or even most of the phenotype' and questioning the implications for understanding aging.

OpenEval evaluates positioning of findings within temporal processing literature (C184) as SUPPORTED, noting novel evidence for dSPN involvement. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this contextualization claim.
